newsitem.title: ZAIRE: UN demands answers over missing Hutu refugees.
newsitem.headline: UN demands answers over missing Hutu refugees.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency has demanded an answer from Zaire rebels on the fate of 55,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees gone missing from a camp.
A U.N. team found Kasese camp set in jungle 25 km (15 miles) south of Kisangani entirely devoid of refugees, though it was teeming last week.

"I am absolutely shocked. There was a camp here a few days ago. People were sick, hungry and too weak to walk. Now where are they?," Filippo Grandi, head of UNHCR's operation in East Zaire asked late on Thursday.
"We are very concerned about their lives and we need answers from the rebels about their fate. In 15 years of my career as an aid worker I have never seen anything like this," Grandi told reporters.
Up to 9,000 of the Kasese refugees were medically unfit to walk when aid workers last visited the camp at the weekend including 2,500 severely malnourished children, according to UNHCR figures.
Sustained automatic gunfire prevented a U.N. team and journalists from proceeding to Biaro Camp further south of Kisangani where up to 25,000 refugees languished last week.

The firing which included bursts of heavy machine gun fire and occasional grenade blasts was billed by Alliance officials as a battle against former Rwandan government troops, but appeared a show by rebels to deter further enquiry.
Journalists attempting to explore the camp found an empty trench, freshly dug, but were unable to explore further because of the fire.
U.N. and Alliance officials were stunned into silence by the sight of the empty camp, unwilling to explain how it could have emptied.
One U.N. staffer picked up the registration card of a young girl and said: "I want to know where is this girl?" Another described the sight as "devestating".
"You saw what we saw. We left in a hurry with you. We want to get all the information together and then we can talk," said Emmanuel Kamanzi, Alliance rebels' delegate to U.N. agencies.

Not a single Rwandan refugee -- dead or alive -- remained visible at Kasese camp. Last week bodies draped in blankets had been laid out in lines and many sick refugees were too weak to walk even one step.
Tutsi-dominated rebels sealed off the Kasese and Biaro camps from aid workers and journalists on Monday, saying they were conducting a military operation.

Rebels agreed to allow the U.N. mission to the camps only after U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said he was "shocked and appalled by the inhumanity" of their action which he said was killing refugees by starvation.
Aid workers had feared that many of the 80,000 Rwandan refugees south of Kisangani had fled because of fighting in the area on Tuesday between rebels, local villagers and refugees.

Zairean villagers said on Wednesday Tutsi-dominated rebels had killed hundreds of Rwandan Hutu refugees at Kasese and a battle between rebels and refugees accompanied the slaughter and an aid worker said he had a report 500 were killed.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila dismissed the reports as "total nonsense", saying Rwandan Hutu militiamen among the refugees attacked villagers and rebels intervened to stop the fighting.
Aid workers accuse rebels of orchestrating attacks on aid vehicles and looting of aid since Friday after delaying until May 5 a U.N. airlift of up to 100,000 refugees in the region.
The Hutus included members of the former Rwandan government and extremist Interahamwe militia who played a leading role in the 1994 genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
They arrived at Kasese and Biaro in mid-March after six months of trekking over volcanic rock and through thick bush and jungle in a vain attempt to flee the Tutsi-dominated rebels.
